text:
# The Score

My mother lives in Orosi, California, in a stucco two-bedroom with a carport and a swamp cooler on the roof that groans like a ship. She bought it in 1971 with my father's life insurance, which was not much, and she has outlived the roof twice. When I called to say I was coming down for a Saturday in June, she said, "Well, don't come for my sake," which is what she says when she means the opposite, and also, sometimes, when she means exactly that.

I drove down from Sacramento Friday night and stayed at the Best Western in Visalia, because my old room is full of what she calls "the inventory": unsold Avon, a sewing machine, three decades of *National Geographic* that a man from the library has been coming to collect since the first Bush administration.

I got to her house at eight-fifteen. She was on the porch in a cardigan, though it was seventy-eight degrees and climbing.

"You're late," she said.

"I said around eight."

"Around eight is eight." She looked me over. "You've lost weight in your face. Are you sick?"

"I'm fifty-three, Ma."

"That's not an answer. I made eggs."

She had made eight eggs, a pound of bacon, and a stack of toast buttered in advance, so it had gone soft and translucent in the middle. It is the only way I have ever liked toast, and I have never been able to reproduce it, because the secret is apparently to be someone else, in another kitchen, with time to waste. She ate one egg and watched me eat the rest.

The kitchen had not changed since I left for college. The same rooster-shaped spoon rest. The same calendar from Garcia's Pharmacy, which had closed in 2009, so the calendar was from 2009, turned to July.

---

After breakfast she did the *Fresno Bee* crossword, in pen, as she does every day. I sat on the arm of the couch, the way I used to at twelve.

"Seven letters," she said. "'Opposite of zenith.'"

"Nadir."

"That's five."

"Then I don't know."

She wrote something in. I leaned over. She had written NADIRRR.

"Ma."

"It fits," she said. "It's my puzzle."

We did the whole thing that way, her inventing words, me correcting her, her ignoring me. Halfway through she handed me the pen, so the bottom half is in my handwriting, smaller and slanting the wrong way, and next to some of my answers she drew little question marks, as though I were the one making things up.

Around eleven she said she had to go to the post office. She has had a box since 1974, though the mailman delivers to her house six days a week. She keeps it, as far as I can tell, so she has somewhere to walk. It is nine blocks. In summer, at noon, those nine blocks are like walking across the floor of a kiln.

"I'll drive you," I said.

"I don't need to be driven."

"I know. I'd like to."

She decided, I think, that this was a concession she could afford once. The box contained a gutter-cleaning flyer and a card from her dentist about an appointment she had already missed. She read both carefully, standing at the little window, as though they were letters from abroad.

On the way back I drove past the house on Avenue 416, where we'd lived before my father died. It was green now, with a chain-link fence and a trampoline.

"They took out the fig tree," she said. "You used to eat the figs before they were ripe and be sick all night. Every summer, you never learned. Your father thought it was funny. I was the one up with you."

"I don't remember that."

"No," she said. "You wouldn't."

---

In the afternoon we played gin rummy under the ceiling fan, with cards so old the jacks had worn faces. She keeps score on a yellow legal pad, in two columns, to five hundred. She cheats. She has always cheated, badly and openly, picking up out of turn, laying down runs that skip a number, and when I point it out she says, "Oh, is that how we're playing," as if I've proposed some fussy new house rule.

Around the third hand I stopped pointing it out. It was easier, and there was something about watching her slip the seven of hearts into a run of clubs, glancing up to see if I'd noticed, that made me feel, briefly, not like a fifty-three-year-old man with a bad knee and a divorce, but like a child who was being gotten away with.

"You're letting me win," she said, at about three hundred and forty.

"You're cheating."

"Same thing," she said, and laid down a run of spades with a diamond in the middle.

At four she got up to water the tomatoes, which she grows in five-gallon chlorine buckets along the back fence. The thermometer on the carport post said a hundred and four.

"Wear a hat," I said. There was a straw hat on the hook by the back door, wide-brimmed, with a faded blue ribbon. It had been hers for twenty years. I had never seen her wear it.

"That's for show," she said.

"For who?"

"For whoever sees it." She went out bareheaded. I watched her through the window over the sink, small and bent in her cardigan, pressing her thumb over the hose to make it spray, the way she had when my sister and I were small, chasing us around the yard while we screamed.

When she came in, her face was red and she was breathing hard. I gave her water. She drank half and set the glass on the windowsill.

"We didn't finish the game," she said.

"I have to get on the road."

"You'll come back and finish it."

"I'll come back."

She tore off the score sheet, folded it, and put it under the rooster spoon rest. "Then I'll keep this," she said, "so you can't say I made it up."

At the door she hugged me briefly, as though hugging were a toll you paid on the way out of a building. "Drive safe. Don't stop in Fresno, it's all meth now." And then, as I walked to the car: "Wear a hat!"

---

Five weeks later, on a Tuesday in July, Phyllis from next door called me at work. My mother had walked to the post office at noon. Three blocks from home she had sat down on the curb in front of the Iglesia de Cristo and then lain down, and a man coming out of the church had found her. Her temperature in the ambulance was a hundred and six. The hospital in Visalia said *heatstroke*, though Phyllis kept calling it sunstroke, which is what my mother would have called it too.

She was in the ICU for four days. When I got there she was asleep, very small, her hands spotted and bruised from the IVs. When she woke she looked at me a long time and said, "Did you bring my glasses?" I said I hadn't, and she said, "Well, what good are you," and closed her eyes. The nurse said this was a good sign.

The doctor said she would need to go somewhere afterward. He said "rehabilitation" in a way that made it clear the word had been chosen carefully. He asked if she lived alone. I said yes. He wrote something down.

---

I went to the house the next afternoon for her glasses, her nightgowns, and her pills.

Phyllis let me in and stayed on the porch, as though there were something private inside she didn't want to witness. "I watered the tomatoes," she said. "I didn't know what else to do."

The house was hot and smelled the way it always had, of Jergens lotion and coffee and old paper. The kitchen was clean, but in the drying rack was the mug I'd used five weeks earlier, from a bank in Reno, washed and never put away.

The *Fresno Bee* from that Saturday was still on the arm of the recliner. NADIRRR. My slanted letters, her question marks. She had gone back and filled in the last three answers in her own hand. They were words, they fit the spaces; they just weren't the words the puzzle wanted.

On the windowsill over the sink was a glass with an inch of cloudy water in it. I couldn't be sure it was the same glass. I was almost sure.

I found the glasses, the nightgowns, the pills, and put them in a Raley's bag. Then I lifted the rooster spoon rest. The score sheet was there. Her column, my column, three hundred and forty to two hundred and ninety. Underneath, in blue ink, she had written: *Game called on account of son leaving. To be continued.* And below that, in the same blue ink, she had added fifteen points to her own total.

I sat down at the table. Through the window the tomatoes were ripening in their buckets, red and split from the heat, and Phyllis was still on the porch with her arms folded, looking at the street, giving me time.

I put the score sheet in my shirt pocket and took the hat off the hook. It was lighter than I expected. The ribbon had faded almost to white on the side that faced the screen door, and inside the band, in faded marker, someone—my father, I think; it was his handwriting, which I had not seen in fifty years—had written her name, as if she were a child going off to camp, as if there were any danger of her losing it.

I put it in the bag with the nightgowns. She would say she didn't want it. She would say it was for show. I thought I'd bring the cards, too, and the legal pad, and let her cheat as much as she liked.
